title: Everyday CBT

chapters.title: One event, several experiences
chapters.story: Three people interpret the same cancelled invitation differently.
chapters.learn: Explore the connections between situations, thoughts, feelings, bodily sensations, and behaviour.
chapters.lab: Build a five-part map and separate what happened from what someone inferred.

pages.title: One event, several experiences
paragraphs: Alex, Nia, and Jules meet at a Saturday drawing group. One afternoon the organiser writes: “We need to cancel next week.” There is no explanation in the message.

Alex thinks, “Maybe hardly anyone wanted to come,” feels disappointed, and leaves the group chat unopened. Nia thinks, “I have a free afternoon,” feels relieved, and plans some rest. Jules thinks, “Did I cause a problem?” and sends an apologetic message.

Everyone reads the same message. Their thoughts, feelings and actions differ. We do not yet know why the organiser cancelled. Begin by describing each person’s experience without deciding whose reaction is justified.
key_messages: The organiser cancels next week’s drawing group without giving a reason.
Alex thinks people may not want to come, feels disappointed and leaves the chat unopened.
Nia sees a free afternoon and plans to rest. Jules wonders if they caused the cancellation and sends an apology.
An observation describes what happened. An interpretation is what someone thinks it means.

pages.title: Start with what is known
paragraphs: An observation describes what happened. An interpretation suggests what it means. Which statement can you verify directly from the organiser’s message?

options.text: The organiser sent a message cancelling next week’s group.
options.feedback: This describes something that could be checked in the message. It leaves the organiser’s reasons open.

options.text: The organiser no longer likes the group.
options.feedback: This is a possible explanation, but the message does not establish it. Treat it as an interpretation to examine.

options.text: Jules must have done something wrong.
options.feedback: This is Jules’s worry presented as a fact. Their distress matters, but it does not establish responsibility.

pages.title: Five parts, one experience
paragraphs: A situation is a specific event or circumstance. A thought is an interpretation, prediction, memory, or image. An emotion is a feeling such as sadness or anxiety. Bodily sensations include a tight stomach or warmth in the face. Behaviour is what a person does, including withdrawing or asking a question.

These parts influence one another. A racing heart can make a situation feel threatening; leaving can bring relief and change what happens next. The map is a working description, not proof that a thought caused every feeling. Sleep, pain, money, relationships, and other circumstances also matter.
key_messages: Map five parts of one moment. The situation is what happened. A thought gives it meaning, and an emotion names a feeling.
Bodily sensations include a tight stomach or a racing heart. Behaviour is what someone does.
Each part can influence the others.
Use the map as a first account you can revise. Health and circumstances also matter.

pages.title: Make the map specific
paragraphs: “My week was awful” is too broad to investigate. “At three o’clock I read the cancellation message” gives us a moment to examine. “I feel rejected” can contain both an emotion and an interpretation: sadness is the feeling; “they do not want me there” is the meaning.

A map is a hypothesis you can correct. Ask what the person noticed rather than assigning thoughts to them. The first useful change may be practical: checking whether the session will be rescheduled, arranging rest, or asking for information.

items.label: Ask
items.detail: What did it mean to them?

key_messages: Start with one moment, such as reading the message at three o’clock.
“I feel rejected” can combine sadness with the thought “They don’t want me there.” Write the feeling and thought separately.
Ask about their experience; leave missing information open.
A useful next step may be practical, such as checking a new date.

pages.title: A map with room for uncertainty
paragraphs: Jules writes: Situation: the group was cancelled. Thought: “My request for different materials annoyed the organiser.” Feeling: anxiety. Body: tight stomach. Behaviour: sending an apology before finding out why.

Jules changes “I caused the cancellation” to “I am predicting that my request caused it.” That small wording change preserves the concern while acknowledging uncertainty. It does not require Jules to feel calm or believe that everything is fine.
key_messages: Jules thinks their request for different materials might have annoyed the organiser. They feel anxious and notice a tight stomach.
An apology follows before the organiser’s reason is known.
“I’m predicting my request caused this” records the concern and leaves the reason open.

pages.title: Try it in another setting
paragraphs: A colleague walks past without saying hello. You feel hurt. Which next description gives you the most useful starting point?

options.text: They deliberately ignored me because they dislike me.
options.feedback: This combines an observation with an untested intention. You can record the possibility without treating it as established.

options.text: They walked past; I thought they were avoiding me; I felt hurt and stopped approaching them.
options.feedback: This separates the event, interpretation, feeling, and action. You can now examine what is known and what could be checked.

options.text: I should not feel hurt because it is probably nothing.
options.feedback: This dismisses the feeling and replaces one uncertain explanation with another. Understanding comes before judging the reaction.

pages.title: Explain it without looking
paragraphs: Take a moment to answer in your own words before revealing the suggested reasoning.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a thought from an emotion?
questions.answer: A thought carries meaning, such as “I am unwanted.” An emotion names a feeling, such as sadness. Both can be present in the same moment.

questions.prompt: Why is a five-part map provisional?
questions.answer: It records what is currently understood. The person may remember more, clarify their meaning, or learn new facts. It does not capture every cause.

pages.title: Lab: map one moment
paragraphs: Use Jules’s cancellation story, or choose a mild everyday situation you are comfortable considering. Keep to one moment. Personal disclosure is optional.
fields: What happened that another person could observe?
What thought or image appeared?
Which feelings and bodily sensations were present?
What did the person do next?
What is known, and what remains an interpretation?
pages.example:
Event — The organiser cancelled next week’s group and gave no reason.
Thought — Jules wondered whether their request had caused it.
Feeling and body — Jules felt anxious and noticed a tight stomach.
Action — Jules sent an apology.
Known and unknown — The cancellation is confirmed. The reason is unknown.
pages.review: Check that the event and its meaning are separate. You do not need to change a feeling to complete the map.
pages.comparison: Compare your event and thought fields. Which words describe what the message confirms? Which words describe Jules’s explanation?

sources.title: CCI: depression resources — thinking and feeling

chapters.evidence_note: The five-part map is a teaching aid for describing connections. A brief fictional case can illustrate a working explanation and leave other causes open.

chapters.title: How a pattern keeps going
chapters.story: Repeatedly checking work brings brief relief, then another wave of doubt.
chapters.learn: Trace triggers, consequences, and the difference between short-term relief and longer-term effects.
chapters.lab: Draw a maintenance cycle and identify a possible point of change.

pages.title: How a pattern keeps going
paragraphs: Alex volunteers to update the drawing group’s non-critical signup list. They check the dates, then check again. For a moment the worry eases. A few minutes later Alex thinks, “What if I missed something?”

After the sixth check, the list is unchanged but Alex has missed a planned break. “I only finished because I kept checking,” Alex concludes. We need to examine what each check achieves now and what it might make harder later.
key_messages: Alex repeatedly checks an ordinary signup list, despite finding no changes.
Each check briefly eases worry; doubt soon returns.
By the sixth check, Alex has missed a break.
Investigate what checking achieves now and what it costs later.

pages.title: Look at the consequence
paragraphs: What information would best help explain the repeated checking?

options.text: Whether Alex is a perfectionist by nature.
options.feedback: A label may sound explanatory but does not show how this particular pattern works. Look at triggers and consequences.

options.text: What happens to the worry immediately after checking, and when doubt returns.
options.feedback: This can reveal a short-term reward and a longer-term cost. The explanation remains a hypothesis to test.

options.text: Whether the list is perfectly accurate.
options.feedback: Accuracy matters, but it cannot by itself explain why another check feels necessary after no changes. Both task demands and consequences matter.

pages.title: Relief can strengthen a response
paragraphs: When a behaviour removes something unpleasant, a person may become more likely to repeat it. Psychologists call this negative reinforcement. “Negative” means removal here; it is not a judgment about the person.

Alex’s check briefly removes doubt. The next time doubt appears, another check seems attractive. This does not mean all checking is unhelpful: a proportionate check can prevent an actual error. The question is the function and cost of the extra checks in this context.
key_messages: Negative reinforcement means an action may become more likely if it removes something unpleasant, such as doubt.
Brief relief may help keep Alex’s checking loop going.
A first check can catch a real error. Ask what later checks add and what they cost, such as time for a break.

pages.title: Choose a point of influence
paragraphs: A maintenance cycle describes what may keep a current difficulty going. It is different from a life history explaining how the difficulty began. Several influences can operate at once.

Alex could agree a clear, ordinary checking standard with the organiser, then observe what happens after following it. The aim is to learn, not to ban checking everywhere. Checking instructions for a medical, legal, or safety-critical task would require the proper standards for that task.
key_messages: A maintenance cycle describes what may keep a pattern going now.
A separate question is how the pattern began.
Alex can agree with the organiser which checks the signup list needs before testing a change.
Genuine safety requirements still apply.

pages.title: Alex’s first working hypothesis
paragraphs: Alex records three occasions: after a check, worry falls briefly; later it returns despite no new information. That pattern fits the idea that relief helps maintain the repetition. It does not prove the explanation is complete.

For this ordinary signup list, Alex and the organiser agree to check names against the source once and review changed entries. Alex follows that plan, then records the outcome. If the standard misses important errors, they revise the process rather than declaring the experiment a personal failure.
key_messages: On three occasions, a check brings brief relief. Doubt returns even though Alex has no new information.
Alex and the organiser agree to check names against the original list once and review any changed entries.
After following the agreed checks, Alex can see whether the list still contains important errors and adjust the process if needed.

pages.title: A different loop
paragraphs: Nia repeatedly asks a friend whether a short message sounded rude. The reassurance lasts only minutes. What would best clarify the pattern?

options.text: Ask the friend to promise the message could not offend anyone.
options.feedback: A stronger promise might bring relief but cannot guarantee every response. It may leave the same need for reassurance in place.

options.text: Decide that asking for support is always a problem.
options.feedback: Support can be valuable. The relevant question is whether repeated reassurance is providing new information or mainly brief relief.

options.text: Record the trigger, reassurance, immediate relief, and return of doubt.
options.feedback: This distinguishes a possible maintenance loop from a blanket judgment about support. It also leaves room for a practical communication problem.

pages.title: Explain it without looking
paragraphs: Take a moment to answer in your own words before revealing the suggested reasoning.

questions.prompt: What does negative reinforcement mean here?
questions.answer: A behaviour becomes more likely because it removes something unpleasant, such as doubt. It does not mean punishment.

questions.prompt: How does a maintenance explanation differ from an origin story?
questions.answer: It focuses on present triggers and consequences that may sustain a pattern, even when the pattern began for other reasons.

pages.title: Lab: follow the loop
paragraphs: Use Alex’s signup list. Describe a loop with four parts, then identify one small point that could be investigated.
fields: What starts the sequence?
What does Alex do?
What changes immediately?
What happens later, including any cost?
What task-appropriate change could be tested?
pages.example:
Trigger — Alex doubts whether an entry is correct.
Action — Alex checks the unchanged list again.
Immediate effect — Doubt briefly eases.
Later effect — The doubt returns and Alex misses a break.
Possible test — Agree which checks this signup list needs, then see whether following that standard catches important errors.
pages.review: Check that your proposed change fits the task. A cycle is a working explanation, not a label for the person.
pages.comparison: Compare your immediate and later effects. How could brief relief make another check seem useful even when the list stays the same?

sources.title: CCI: perfectionism — what keeps it going?

chapters.evidence_note: This example illustrates a possible reinforcement process. Repetitive checking can have different functions; this course does not assess or treat compulsive symptoms.

chapters.title: Catching the thought
chapters.story: After a small mistake, someone withdraws from the rest of the day.
chapters.learn: Notice automatic thoughts, mental images, and the personal meaning of a moment.
chapters.lab: Reconstruct a specific moment and identify the thought closest to the emotional shift.

pages.title: Catching the thought
paragraphs: Jules notices a wrong date on a poster they helped make. Someone quietly points it out. Jules says, “No problem,” then stays silent for the rest of the session.

Later Jules remembers a sudden image: everyone looking at the poster and shaking their heads. The words were, “I always let people down.” The visible mistake was small; the personal meaning was much larger.
key_messages: When someone points out the wrong date on the poster, Jules says “No problem” and grows quiet.
Jules pictures everyone shaking their heads and thinks, “I always let people down.”
The specific mistake and its wider personal meaning are different things.

pages.title: Ask about the moment
paragraphs: Which question is most likely to uncover the thought linked to Jules’s change in mood?

options.text: When you noticed the date, what went through your mind, including any image?
options.feedback: This invites Jules’s own recollection at the specific moment, without supplying a conclusion.

options.text: You knew they all disliked the poster, didn’t you?
options.feedback: This leads Jules toward an interpretation the questioner has invented. The person’s actual meaning could be different.

options.text: Why are you always so hard on yourself?
options.feedback: This generalises and may sound blaming. A specific moment is easier to investigate than a judgment about character.

pages.title: A thought can arrive as a picture
paragraphs: Automatic thoughts often arrive quickly, before someone deliberately reasons through a situation. They can be words, images, or a sense of what will happen. “Everyone judging the poster” is an image carrying the prediction “They see me as unreliable.”

To notice a thought, return to a manageable moment: what happened, when did the feeling shift, and what did it seem to mean? If nothing comes to mind, leave the space open. You do not have to invent a thought to make the model fit.

diagram.title: From a moment to its meaning

key_messages: Automatic thoughts arrive quickly, before you deliberately think something through. They can be words, images, memories or predictions.
Return to the moment when the feeling changed and ask what it meant.
If no thought comes to mind, write down what you remember and leave the rest open.

pages.title: Name the meaning without endorsing it
paragraphs: “I am a failure” is a thought, not a diagnosis or a fact established by feeling ashamed. Recording “I had the thought that I am a failure” can help distinguish the experience from the conclusion.

Thinking patterns such as overgeneralising or mind-reading can be useful descriptions. They are not a checklist for proving someone irrational. Start with the exact thought, the context, and the evidence. A real mistake can coexist with a much broader conclusion that needs checking.

diagram.title: Keep the scale of the claim visible

items.label: Specific fact
items.detail: One poster has a wrong date

key_messages: “I had the thought that I am a failure” names a thought so you can examine whether the evidence supports it.
Overgeneralising means drawing a broad conclusion from limited evidence. Mind-reading means assuming you know what someone else thinks.
Keep a specific error separate from a broad judgment about the person.

pages.title: A more precise record
paragraphs: Jules initially writes “I felt useless.” They clarify the feeling as shame and the thought as “If I make a visible mistake, people cannot rely on me.” Their shoulders tense, and they stop offering help.

Jules can now address two things: correcting the date and examining the prediction about reliability. The map does not erase the mistake. It prevents one error from silently becoming a complete verdict on their worth.
key_messages: Jules identifies shame as the feeling and “People cannot rely on me” as the thought.
Tense shoulders and withdrawing are other parts of the experience.
There are two tasks for Jules. Correct the poster date and ask what the mistake actually shows about reliability.

pages.title: Find the thought
paragraphs: Alex says, “I felt anxious before the group because I pictured being unable to speak.” Which part is the automatic thought?

options.text: The word anxious.
options.feedback: Anxious names an emotion. It is useful information, but it does not describe the prediction or image.

options.text: The image of being unable to speak.
options.feedback: An image can carry a prediction just as words can. Ask what Alex believed the image meant or would lead to.

options.text: The fact that Alex attended the group.
options.feedback: Attending is behaviour. It may be relevant to the map, but it is not the image Alex described.

pages.title: Explain it without looking
paragraphs: Take a moment to answer in your own words before revealing the suggested reasoning.

questions.prompt: Must an automatic thought be a sentence?
questions.answer: No. It can appear as an image, memory, or prediction. Ask what it means to the person.

questions.prompt: What should you do if no thought is recalled?
questions.answer: Record what is known and leave uncertainty. Do not manufacture a thought or insist that every bodily reaction has a clear verbal cause.

pages.title: Lab: slow down one moment
paragraphs: Use Jules’s poster story. Find the smallest specific moment at which the emotion changed.
fields: What was happening just before the feeling shifted?
What words or image appeared?
What did that thought imply about Jules or the situation?
Which part is a feeling, and which part is a conclusion?
What practical issue still needs attention?
pages.example:
Moment — Someone points out the wrong date on the poster.
Image — Jules pictures others shaking their heads.
Meaning — “People cannot rely on me.”
Feeling and conclusion — Shame is the feeling. Being unreliable is the conclusion Jules draws.
Practical issue — The poster date still needs correcting.
pages.review: Use the character’s reported meaning. Avoid inferring a hidden belief without evidence.
pages.comparison: Compare your feeling and conclusion fields. Which describes Jules’s experience, and which claim goes beyond the facts of the poster error?

sources.title: CCI: depression resources — automatic thoughts and ABC analysis

chapters.evidence_note: Thought monitoring is an introductory observation skill. It is not an instruction to monitor every thought or analyse distress indefinitely.

chapters.title: Making room for another interpretation
chapters.story: A brief message sounds hostile to the person who receives it.
chapters.learn: Examine evidence, recognise uncertainty, and develop balanced alternatives.
chapters.lab: Complete a short thought record without forcing a reassuring conclusion.

pages.title: Making room for another interpretation
paragraphs: Jules sends Alex a message asking whether a drawing looks unfinished. Six hours pass without a reply. Jules thinks, “Alex is annoyed with me for asking,” and begins drafting an apology.
There has been no argument. Alex sometimes replies late, but yesterday answered another question quickly. Jules feels hurt and uncertain. We have some relevant information and several missing pieces.
key_messages: Alex has not replied to Jules’s drawing question for six hours.
Jules feels hurt, thinks Alex is annoyed by the question and begins writing an apology.
There has been no argument. Alex replied faster yesterday and sometimes replies late. Today’s reason is unknown.

pages.title: Choose a fair alternative
paragraphs: Which statement best preserves what Jules knows and does not know?

options.text: Alex definitely is not annoyed; everything is fine.
options.feedback: That is reassuring, but still claims access to Alex’s mind. A balanced thought should fit the evidence, including uncertainty.

options.text: Six hours proves Alex is annoyed.
options.feedback: A delay is observable; the reason is not established. The conclusion is stronger than the available evidence.

options.text: Alex has not replied. They may be busy or annoyed; I do not yet know why.
options.feedback: This recognises the delay and the uncertainty without demanding a positive conclusion. Jules can choose a practical next step.

pages.title: Evidence is more than a feeling
paragraphs: A thought record separates the event, the thought, the feeling, evidence supporting the thought, evidence that complicates it, and a balanced response. The aim is a fair account, not winning an argument against yourself.

Jules’s feeling is evidence that the situation matters to Jules. It is not direct evidence of Alex’s intention. A previous argument would be relevant evidence; imagining a frown is not an observed response. Evidence may support part of a thought without supporting its strongest version.
key_messages: A thought record separates the event, thought and feeling. It records relevant facts and what you can fairly conclude.
Feeling hurt tells us the delay matters to Jules. Alex’s intention remains unknown.
A disagreement would be relevant evidence if it had happened. A slower reply only shows a change in timing.

pages.title: A balanced response can remain uncomfortable
paragraphs: A balanced response should be believable and specific. “I cannot know the reason from the delay alone” may fit better than “Nobody is ever annoyed with me.” It can include a coping statement: “If there is a disagreement, I can ask about it.”

After reviewing the thought, Jules can choose whether an ordinary follow-up is needed. Repeatedly rewriting a record to reach certainty can become another loop. Set a reasonable stopping point and return to the activity you intended to do.

items.label: Check
items.detail: What facts fit or complicate it?

key_messages: A balanced response should be specific, believable, and open to uncertainty.
It can say what you would do if the concern proved true. “If there is a disagreement, I can ask about it.”
Decide whether an ordinary follow-up would help. Stop reviewing the record once you have a useful next step.

pages.title: Jules writes a balanced response
paragraphs: Jules thinks Alex is annoyed by the request. Alex replied faster yesterday. That is a change in timing and leaves the reason unknown. Alex has replied late before, there has been no argument, and Jules does not know Alex’s schedule today.

Jules writes, “The delay does not tell me why. If I need an answer by tomorrow, I can say when I need it.” Jules still feels some uncertainty. They decide to work on another part of the drawing instead of sending several apologetic messages.
key_messages: Alex’s reply was faster yesterday, and late replies have happened before. The facts establish the delay and leave the reason open.
Jules concludes, “The delay alone does not tell me why.”
If an answer is needed by tomorrow, one ordinary follow-up can state that deadline.

pages.title: When the evidence changes
paragraphs: Alex later says, “I was irritated by the repeated requests, and I was busy.” How should Jules update the record?

options.text: Acknowledge the irritation and discuss a clearer way to ask, without turning it into “Alex rejects me.”
options.feedback: New evidence should change the account. A specific disagreement can call for communication without establishing a global judgment.

options.text: Ignore the message because CBT means choosing the positive explanation.
options.feedback: A fair account must include unwelcome evidence. CBT skills should not require denying a real disagreement.

options.text: Conclude that every future delayed reply means irritation.
options.feedback: One clarified event does not settle the meaning of every future delay. Context still matters.

pages.title: Explain it without looking
paragraphs: Take a moment to answer in your own words before revealing the suggested reasoning.

questions.prompt: What makes a balanced thought different from reassurance?
questions.answer: It fits the available evidence and admits what is unknown. It does not guarantee the preferred outcome.

questions.prompt: What if the difficult interpretation is partly supported?
questions.answer: Update it, keep the claim specific, and consider problem-solving or communication. A real problem does not justify every broader conclusion.

pages.title: Lab: write a short thought record
paragraphs: Use Jules’s unanswered message. Write an initial response before looking at the example.
fields: Specific event and initial thought
Feeling and optional intensity in your own terms
Facts that directly support the thought, if any
Facts that complicate it or remain unknown
A balanced response and a practical next step
pages.example:
Event and thought — Alex has not replied for six hours. Jules thinks Alex is annoyed.
Feeling — Jules feels hurt and uncertain.
Supporting facts — There is no direct evidence of annoyance from the delay. Yesterday’s faster reply is timing information.
Other facts and unknowns — Alex sometimes replies late. Today’s schedule and the reason for the delay are unknown.
Balanced response and action — “I don’t know why Alex hasn’t replied. If I need an answer by tomorrow, I can say so in one follow-up.”
pages.review: Does the response acknowledge difficult possibilities? Does the next step serve a practical purpose rather than seek impossible certainty?
pages.comparison: Compare your evidence and response fields. Does your response leave Alex’s reason open while naming a next step that would help with the drawing?

sources.title: CCI: depression resources — detective work and balanced thoughts

chapters.evidence_note: Thought records are one CBT tool. They are not appropriate for resolving every difficulty, and a plausible alternative is not proof of what another person thinks.

chapters.title: Moving before motivation arrives
chapters.story: A week gradually loses activities that used to provide connection and satisfaction.
chapters.learn: Explore behavioural activation through meaningful, manageable activities.
chapters.lab: Plan one small activity, anticipate obstacles, and review what actually happened.

pages.title: Moving before motivation arrives
paragraphs: Nia’s shifts have been tiring. She stops sketching after work and turns down a short walk with Jules. Rest helps on some evenings, but over two weeks her days contain fewer things she enjoys or values.
Nia keeps thinking, “I will start again when I feel motivated.” The days become more empty, and starting feels harder. She wants to investigate this without treating exhaustion as a character flaw.
key_messages: After tiring shifts, Nia stops sketching and declines a walk.
Some rest helps, but her week now offers fewer valued activities.
Nia is waiting to feel motivated. She wants to find out whether a small activity fits her energy.

pages.title: Make a manageable start
paragraphs: Which plan gives Nia the clearest, most realistic first experiment?

options.text: Fill every evening with activities so there is no time to feel low.
options.feedback: A crowded schedule may ignore exhaustion and be difficult to sustain. More activity is not automatically better.

options.text: Try ten minutes of sketching after a suitable shift, with a smaller version if energy is low.
options.feedback: This specifies a meaningful activity and respects capacity. Nia can observe what follows without needing motivation to arrive first.

options.text: Wait until she is certain the activity will improve her mood.
options.feedback: That certainty is unavailable beforehand. A small, feasible experiment can provide information.

pages.title: Action can create an opportunity
paragraphs: Behavioural activation involves noticing patterns of activity and their consequences, then planning manageable actions that may restore contact with meaningful or rewarding parts of life. Motivation sometimes follows action; it does not always arrive first.

Activities can offer connection, enjoyment, accomplishment, care, or rest. Those experiences may matter even if mood does not improve immediately. Activity planning must fit physical health, responsibilities, resources, and the person’s preferences.
key_messages: Behavioural activation looks at what happens after activities and plans small actions linked to what someone values.
A manageable action can create opportunities for connection, satisfaction, or accomplishment.
Motivation may follow action; an immediate mood improvement is not guaranteed.
Include rest and respect health, resources, and responsibilities.

pages.title: Plan an action you can actually observe
paragraphs: “Be more active” is vague. “After Tuesday’s early shift, put paper on the table and sketch for ten minutes” specifies a cue and a doable action. A two-minute version can help Nia start without making it an all-or-nothing test.

Record what happened before drawing a conclusion. Did the task fit the available energy? Did it offer any interest or accomplishment? Did transport, pain, cost, or another barrier intervene? Review the plan rather than judging the person.

diagram.title: A plan that fits a real day

key_messages: Choose an action, a time and a place. Nia plans ten minutes of sketching at home after an early shift.
Plan a smaller version that fits a low-energy day.
Review feasibility and barriers as well as mood.

pages.title: A mixed result is still information
paragraphs: Nia sketches for six minutes. Her mood does not noticeably change, but she enjoys choosing a colour and wants to finish the drawing another day. She also notices that she had planned it too close to a late shift.

Nia keeps the activity, moves it to a more suitable evening, and protects rest after late shifts. The experiment supports a narrower conclusion than “drawing cures low mood”: a small creative activity can be feasible and worthwhile on some days.
key_messages: Nia sketches for six minutes. Her mood stays the same and she enjoys choosing a colour.
She notices she planned the activity too close to a late shift and decides to try an earlier evening next time.
Keep what is worthwhile, adapt the timing, and protect needed rest.

pages.title: Review the plan fairly
paragraphs: Jules plans a walk but rain and a care commitment prevent it. What is the most useful review?

options.text: The plan proves Jules lacks commitment.
options.feedback: This converts practical barriers into a global judgment and provides little guidance for the next attempt.

options.text: Double the length of tomorrow’s walk as compensation.
options.feedback: An automatic increase may make the next plan less feasible. There is no exercise debt to repay.

options.text: Identify the barriers and choose a smaller or differently timed activity that serves the same purpose.
options.feedback: This treats the outcome as information. It preserves the purpose while adapting to circumstances.

pages.title: Explain it without looking
paragraphs: Take a moment to answer in your own words before revealing the suggested reasoning.

questions.prompt: Why not wait for motivation every time?
questions.answer: A small planned action can create opportunities for interest or connection that waiting may not provide. It is an experiment, not a guarantee.

questions.prompt: What counts as a useful outcome besides improved mood?
questions.answer: Feasibility, connection, satisfaction, accomplishment, or learning about barriers. Rest can also be a meaningful planned action.

pages.title: Lab: plan one meaningful activity
paragraphs: Use Nia’s situation or an optional mild everyday example. Choose something affordable, accessible, and compatible with health and responsibilities.
fields: What purpose would the activity serve?
What small action, when and where?
What is the smaller version?
What barrier might occur, and how could the plan adapt?
Use Nia’s six-minute result or record your own if you tried an activity. What happened, and what would you change?
pages.example:
Purpose — Make room for creativity.
Plan — Sketch at home for ten minutes after an early shift.
Smaller version — Sketch for two minutes if energy is low.
Barrier and adaptation — Protect rest after late shifts. Move drawing to a more suitable evening.
Result and revision — Nia sketched for six minutes and enjoyed choosing a colour. Her mood stayed the same. She plans to change the timing.
pages.review: The plan should fit the person’s actual resources. If low mood or fatigue is persistent or substantially affects daily life, consider support from a qualified professional rather than relying on this course.
pages.comparison: Compare your purpose and result fields. What made the activity worthwhile for Nia, and what did the result suggest changing?

sources.title: CCI: depression resources — behavioural strategies and activity scheduling
NICE NG222: treatment options and individual needs

chapters.evidence_note: Behavioural activation is an established treatment approach when delivered appropriately. This brief activity-planning exercise is introductory education; it is not an evaluated treatment programme.

chapters.title: Solving what can be solved
chapters.story: A real workload problem becomes tangled with predictions about failure.
chapters.learn: Distinguish practical problems from hypothetical worries and work through possible solutions.
chapters.lab: Define a manageable problem, compare options, and choose a concrete next step.

pages.title: Solving what can be solved
paragraphs: Alex has agreed to design a poster, update a signup list, and collect supplies before Saturday. There are only two free evenings. “What if everyone thinks I am unreliable?” keeps running through their mind.
There is a practical capacity problem as well as a prediction about other people’s reactions. Arguing with the prediction will not create another evening. Alex needs to decide what can change.
key_messages: Alex has three tasks to finish before Saturday and only two free evenings.
Alex worries about seeming unreliable. Three tasks and two evenings are also a practical scheduling problem.
Which of the tasks could change in scope, timing or who does the work?

pages.title: Define the problem
paragraphs: Which problem statement is specific enough to work on?

options.text: Three tasks need doing before Saturday, and I have time for about two.
options.feedback: This identifies a current gap and makes possible solutions visible: change scope, timing, or who does the work.

options.text: I am incapable of managing my life.
options.feedback: This global judgment does not identify a changeable task. It may be a thought worth examining separately.

options.text: What if I disappoint everyone forever?
options.feedback: This predicts a broad future outcome. A useful immediate problem statement focuses on the current situation.

pages.title: Separate a current problem from a hypothetical future
paragraphs: A practical problem has a present situation and some possible action. A hypothetical worry asks what might happen, often without a decision that can be made now. The same concern can contain both.

Alex can estimate the work and contact the organiser. Alex cannot guarantee nobody will ever feel disappointed. Useful problem-solving addresses the actionable part, then leaves room for the uncertainty that remains.
key_messages: A practical problem has a current situation and a possible action.
A hypothetical worry asks about a future outcome that may not be settled now.
Address what can change, then acknowledge the uncertainty that remains.

pages.title: Generate options before choosing
paragraphs: Define the goal, list possible approaches, consider costs and feasibility, choose a step, and set a review point. Options can include asking for help, reducing scope, delaying a task, or deciding that a task is not needed.

Problem-solving is not a demand to solve structural problems alone. Some situations require resources, specialist advice, or collective action. A useful step can be identifying who has the authority or support to help.
key_messages: Define a specific goal and generate several options before choosing.
Compare feasibility, resources, costs, and who can help.
Choose a concrete step and a review point.
Some problems need specialist support or collective action.

pages.title: Alex makes a decision with incomplete certainty
paragraphs: Alex estimates the poster at one evening, the list at half an evening, and the supplies trip at another. Options include a simpler poster, another volunteer collecting supplies, or a later deadline.

Alex asks the organiser to prioritise. They agree on the simpler poster and share the collection task. Alex still worries about seeming difficult. The practical issue is better specified even though the feeling has not disappeared.
key_messages: Alex estimates one evening for the poster, half an evening for the list and another evening for supplies.
The organiser agrees to simplify the poster and share the supplies trip, two changes that make the workload more feasible.
The practical plan can improve even while worry remains.

pages.title: Choose the next tool
paragraphs: Nia has sent a complete application and cannot change it before next week’s response. She keeps asking, “What if I am rejected?” What fits now?

options.text: Rewrite the unavailable application in her mind until she feels certain.
options.feedback: This cannot change the submitted application and may extend the loop without producing a decision.

options.text: Check once whether a real next step is available, then practise returning attention while accepting the outcome is unknown.
options.feedback: This distinguishes useful preparation from repeated attempts to obtain certainty. A planned review point may help.

options.text: Assume rejection is impossible because there is nothing more to do.
options.feedback: Lack of an action does not guarantee a preferred result. The skill is making room for uncertainty, not denying it.

pages.title: Explain it without looking
paragraphs: Take a moment to answer in your own words before revealing the suggested reasoning.

questions.prompt: What makes a problem statement workable?
questions.answer: It identifies a specific current situation and a realistic goal, rather than judging the whole person.

questions.prompt: Can a practical solution leave anxiety behind?
questions.answer: Yes. A useful action can address the situation while uncertainty or emotion remains. Feeling calm is not a prerequisite for every decision.

pages.title: Lab: choose a practical next step
paragraphs: Use Alex’s three tasks. Keep the problem within the person’s influence while recognising where help is needed.
fields: State the current problem without a character judgment
Describe a realistic goal
List at least three options
Compare effort, resources, consequences, and fairness
Choose a step, who will act, and a review point
pages.example:
Problem — Three jobs need doing before Saturday and Alex has two free evenings.
Goal — Finish the essential jobs in the time available.
Options — Simplify the poster, share the supplies trip or renegotiate timing.
Comparison — A simpler poster saves time. Sharing the trip depends on another volunteer. A later deadline depends on the organiser.
Step and review — Ask the organiser to set priorities today, then check whether the agreed jobs fit the two evenings.
pages.review: Check that your plan changes something observable. Identify what remains uncertain rather than adding more planning to chase a guarantee.
pages.comparison: Compare your chosen step and review point. What would you look for to decide whether the new plan actually fits two evenings?

chapters.evidence_note: Structured problem-solving is a general skill. Legal, financial, employment, or safeguarding problems may require qualified advice beyond the scope of an introductory course.

chapters.title: Turning a belief into a question
chapters.story: Someone predicts that asking for clarification will make them look incompetent.
chapters.learn: Turn a belief into an observable prediction and learn from mixed evidence.
chapters.lab: Design an experiment with a prediction, an action, and a fair way to interpret the result.

pages.title: Turning a belief into a question
paragraphs: Jules is unsure which paper size the group needs. “If I ask, the organiser will think I am incompetent,” they predict. Guessing would hide the uncertainty but might produce the wrong order.
Jules wants to investigate the prediction in an ordinary, low-stakes interaction. The question needs to be clear enough that the result can teach them something.
key_messages: Jules needs to know which paper size to order.
They predict that asking will make the organiser think they are incompetent.
Jules plans to ask one ordinary question and pay attention to what the organiser says or does.

pages.title: Make the prediction observable
paragraphs: Which prediction about the organiser’s response could Jules check by listening to the words or observing the actions that follow?

options.text: The organiser will secretly judge me.
options.feedback: A private judgment cannot be directly observed in this interaction. Choose indicators while recognising that they cannot reveal every hidden thought.

options.text: Asking will feel completely comfortable.
options.feedback: Jules could observe their own feelings, but this prediction would tell them about comfort and leave the question about the organiser’s response open.

options.text: If I ask one clear question, the organiser will refuse to answer or explicitly criticise me for asking.
options.feedback: This identifies observable responses. It is a narrower claim than knowing what the organiser privately thinks.

pages.title: An experiment asks a question
paragraphs: A behavioural experiment compares a prediction with what happens after an action. Specify the situation, the prediction, what you will do, what you will observe, and how different outcomes could be interpreted.

Choose an ordinary, ethical, low-stakes action. Do not manufacture conflict, put someone at risk, or use an experiment to test a dangerous situation. The aim is useful information rather than proving bravery or forcing a preferred result.

items.label: Action
items.detail: Ask which paper size is needed

key_messages: A behavioural experiment compares a specific prediction with an observed outcome.
Plan the action, observations, and how different results could be interpreted.
Use an ordinary, voluntary situation where no one is put at risk. The goal is to gather useful information.

pages.title: Mixed outcomes need careful interpretation
paragraphs: The organiser might answer warmly, answer briefly, ask Jules to check the written instructions, or criticise the repeated question. Each result supports a different, limited conclusion.

A brief answer does not prove warmth or hostility. One friendly interaction does not establish that criticism can never happen. If an awkward result occurs, examine what it shows about the specific situation and how Jules coped. Avoid turning one trial into a verdict on the person.

items.label: Revise
items.detail: What is the next useful question?

key_messages: Warm, brief, awkward, and critical replies support different conclusions.
A reply cannot reveal every private opinion.
Write down the reply. Did it include a refusal or criticism? What question could you investigate next?

pages.title: Jules gets a brief answer
paragraphs: Jules asks, “For Saturday’s drawings, should I order A3 or A4?” The organiser replies, “A3, thanks,” then returns to another task. No criticism occurs. Jules still feels tense.

The observable prediction of refusal or explicit criticism was not supported in this trial. Jules cannot conclude that the organiser had no private judgment. They learn that asking a clear question was possible while anxious and obtained the information they needed.
key_messages: Jules asks “A3 or A4?” and receives “A3, thanks.”
The predicted refusal or explicit criticism does not occur in this trial.
Jules obtains useful information while still anxious; private judgments remain unknown.

pages.title: Review an awkward outcome
paragraphs: In another experiment, a colleague says, “Please check the instructions first next time.” What is the fairest conclusion?

options.text: The response identifies a specific expectation; examine whether it was reasonable and what to do next.
options.feedback: This accepts the actual feedback without generalising to “I am incompetent.” The experiment can inform a practical adjustment.

options.text: The experiment failed, so there is nothing to learn.
options.feedback: An unwelcome result can still provide useful information about the situation, the prediction, and possible responses.

options.text: This proves every request for clarification will be rejected.
options.feedback: One response cannot establish what every person will do in every context. Keep the conclusion at the scale of the evidence.

pages.title: Explain it without looking
paragraphs: Take a moment to answer in your own words before revealing the suggested reasoning.

questions.prompt: Why specify an observable prediction?
questions.answer: It makes comparison possible and reduces the temptation to interpret any outcome as proof of a hidden judgment.

questions.prompt: Does a useful experiment have to disconfirm the prediction?
questions.answer: No. Supporting or mixed evidence can inform an updated understanding, a practical change, or a different question.

pages.title: Lab: design a fair test
paragraphs: Use Jules’s paper order. You can design the experiment without carrying it out. If choosing your own example, keep it ordinary, voluntary, and safe.
fields: What specific prediction will you investigate?
What action, setting, and time?
What observations would support or complicate the prediction?
What could make the result hard to interpret?
If you are planning only, use the reply “A3, thanks.” Which part of the prediction fits this reply, what remains unknown, and what would you revise?
pages.example:
Prediction — The organiser will refuse to answer or criticise Jules for asking.
Action — Ask once whether the group needs A3 or A4 paper.
Observations — Record the answer or refusal and any explicit words of criticism.
Limit — The organiser’s private thoughts are unknown.
Example result — The organiser says “A3, thanks.” Jules receives an answer without explicit criticism. A future reply may be different.
pages.review: Check that the test can teach something even if the result is mixed. Feelings matter, but they are not the only outcome measure.
pages.comparison: Compare your prediction and result. Which part of the predicted response occurred, and what could the reply never tell you about the organiser’s private opinion?

chapters.evidence_note: Behavioural experiments are used across CBT approaches. This lesson illustrates the reasoning process; individual experiments may need adaptation and professional guidance.

chapters.title: Approaching what feels difficult
chapters.story: Avoiding ordinary social situations makes them increasingly daunting.
chapters.learn: Explore avoidance, safety behaviours, and gradual approach in safe everyday situations.
chapters.lab: Build a voluntary ladder of manageable steps, with room to adjust the pace.

pages.title: Approaching what feels difficult
paragraphs: Alex wants to talk to new people at the drawing group. They arrive late, look busy with their phone, and leave before the break. This lowers the immediate chance of an awkward greeting, but also limits the conversations they want.
Alex does not want to deliver a speech. They want a manageable way to practise an ordinary greeting in a group they have chosen to attend.
key_messages: Alex wants to talk to people. Arriving late, looking busy on their phone and leaving before the break make a greeting less likely.
Avoiding greetings reduces Alex’s chances of an awkward moment and also limits chances to talk.
Alex chooses to practise one manageable greeting.

pages.title: Choose a first step
paragraphs: Which first step gives Alex a manageable way to practise the greeting they want to try?

options.text: Give an unprepared speech to everyone immediately.
options.feedback: A much larger task may not fit the goal or readiness. A useful step can be small and agreed voluntarily.

options.text: Arrive at the usual time and say hello to one familiar person, then review the experience.
options.feedback: This creates a manageable opportunity for learning and connection. It can be adjusted if it does not fit.

options.text: Keep avoiding the break until all anxiety has disappeared.
options.feedback: Waiting for no anxiety may leave the same avoidance pattern in place. Alex can consider a manageable step with some discomfort.

pages.title: Avoidance changes what you can learn
paragraphs: Avoidance can bring short-term relief while reducing opportunities to discover how a situation unfolds or how a person can cope. This is one reason gradual approach is used in CBT for some fears.

Avoiding actual danger can be sensible. A safe everyday social situation is different from harassment, unsafe conditions, or an activity that conflicts with medical advice. Choose the context carefully and keep the person in control.

items.label: Step 2
items.detail: Ask a familiar member a question

key_messages: Avoidance can reduce discomfort while limiting opportunities to learn.
A voluntary ladder divides a chosen goal into manageable steps.
Approach safe everyday situations; do not use the model to dismiss actual danger.

pages.title: Review learning, not a courage score
paragraphs: A ladder divides a chosen goal into steps that differ in difficulty. The order is personal, not a ranking imposed by someone else. Repeating, adjusting, or seeking support can be appropriate.

Safety behaviours are actions intended to prevent a feared outcome that may also make it harder to discover what happens without them. Hiding behind a phone may serve that function for Alex. Disability aids, necessary accommodations, and genuine safety precautions should not be removed on that basis. Ask about the function before making changes.
key_messages: Choose the pace personally; repeat or adapt a step when useful.
A safety behaviour is an action meant to prevent a feared outcome. It can make it harder to tell what would happen without it.
Preserve necessary accommodations, access aids, and genuine safety precautions.
Ask what the action does for this person in this situation. A phone can be cover or a way to make communication accessible.

pages.title: Alex tries one greeting
paragraphs: Alex chooses to greet a familiar member at the start. Their voice feels shaky. The member says hello and asks about the drawing. Alex stays for two minutes, then returns to their materials.

Alex records that greeting was possible with some anxiety and led to a brief exchange. They decide to repeat the same step once more before considering a new one. They do not need to report zero anxiety or reach the top of a ladder on a fixed schedule.
key_messages: Alex greets a familiar member despite a shaky voice and has a brief exchange.
The learning is that a greeting was possible with some anxiety.
Alex chooses to repeat the greeting and decides when another step might fit.

pages.title: Keep the context in view
paragraphs: Nia avoids a group where someone has repeatedly harassed her. What is the most appropriate starting point?

options.text: Use the same approach ladder because all avoidance maintains fear.
options.feedback: This ignores evidence of real harm. A general model must not override the actual circumstances.

options.text: Remove every source of support so the experiment is pure.
options.feedback: Support and accommodations can protect access and safety. Removing them indiscriminately is not a useful learning goal.

options.text: Consider safety, boundaries, and appropriate support before any decision about returning.
options.feedback: A real threat calls for a contextual response. Nia does not owe the group an exposure exercise.

pages.title: Explain it without looking
paragraphs: Take a moment to answer in your own words before revealing the suggested reasoning.

questions.prompt: Why can avoidance maintain a fear?
questions.answer: It may reduce immediate discomfort while limiting opportunities to test predictions or learn how to cope.

questions.prompt: How is an accommodation different from a safety behaviour?
questions.answer: An accommodation may provide necessary access or protection. Function and context matter; the same outward action cannot be classified from appearance alone.

pages.title: Lab: build a voluntary ladder
paragraphs: Use Alex’s ordinary greeting goal. Designing a fictional ladder is enough. Do not use this exercise for dangerous situations, trauma memories, or severe symptoms without appropriate professional support.
fields: What chosen goal would the steps serve?
What is a manageable first step?
What two or three later steps might fit?
Which supports or accommodations should remain?
What learning would you review, and how could you adjust the pace?
pages.example:
Goal — Have more everyday conversations at the group.
First step — Greet a familiar member.
Later steps — Ask a familiar member a question, then consider greeting a new member.
Support — Keep any communication and access aids Alex needs.
Review — Record whether the greeting was possible and what happened. Alex can repeat or adjust the step.
pages.review: Each step should remain voluntary and fit the person’s context. A harder step is not automatically a better one.
pages.comparison: Compare your goal and first step. What could Alex learn even if their voice still shakes? Which supports would help them take part?

sources.title: CCI: social anxiety — avoidance, stepladders, and safety behaviours

chapters.evidence_note: This chapter introduces gradual approach in safe everyday situations. It is not an exposure protocol for a diagnosed condition and does not replace individual assessment.

chapters.title: When thinking becomes a loop
chapters.story: An awkward conversation becomes the subject of a whole evening of repeated analysis.
chapters.learn: Distinguish useful reflection from worry and rumination, and practise shifting attention.
chapters.lab: Notice a thinking loop, assess whether it is producing useful information, and choose where to put attention next.

pages.title: When thinking becomes a loop
paragraphs: After the drawing group, Nia remembers a joke that received little response. She replays it on the bus, at dinner, and while preparing for bed. Each replay asks, “Why did I say that?” but produces no new information.
Nia would like to learn from social mistakes. She also notices that tonight’s analysis is taking time away from rest without reaching a decision.
key_messages: Nia repeatedly replays a joke that received little response.
The question “Why did I say that?” produces no new information or decision.
The replays take time away from rest. Nia wants to tell whether there is a useful action to take.

pages.title: Reflection or repetition?
paragraphs: Which question best distinguishes useful reflection from a thinking loop?

options.text: Is this producing new information or a specific decision I can act on?
options.feedback: This looks at the function of the thinking. A repeated question without new information may call for a different response.

options.text: Have I thought about it for exactly the right number of minutes?
options.feedback: Time can be a clue, but there is no universal minute limit that separates helpful and unhelpful thinking.

options.text: Can I force myself never to think about it again?
options.feedback: Trying to eliminate a thought can create another struggle. The skill is choosing how to respond when it appears.

pages.title: Thinking can become an activity of its own
paragraphs: Worry often concerns what might happen; rumination often returns to what happened or what it means about oneself. They can overlap. The useful question is whether the thinking helps a decision or keeps circling without one.

A difficult thought returning does not mean the person chose it or failed. Notice its arrival, name the process gently, and consider whether something useful can be done. If there is a practical issue, use a defined problem-solving step.

items.label: Memory
items.detail: A quiet response to the joke

key_messages: Worry often concerns what could happen. Rumination means repeatedly going over the past or what it says about you.
Ask whether thinking produces new information or a useful decision.
When a thought returns, notice it and check for one useful action.

pages.title: Return attention without demanding an empty mind
paragraphs: Nia can acknowledge, “That conversation is back in my mind,” check whether an action is needed, and deliberately return attention to a chosen activity. The thought may remain in the background. The aim is flexible attention rather than thought suppression.

Choose something concrete: notice the feel of a brush, follow a paragraph, or listen to a person speaking. When attention wanders, return again without treating it as a test. If a real repair is needed, decide on one proportionate action rather than rehearsing indefinitely.

diagram.title: A different response to the replay

items.label: Choose
items.detail: Act once, or leave it unresolved

key_messages: Notice the replay and check for a practical action.
Then return attention to a chosen activity, even if the thought remains.
Flexible attention means returning to the activity you chose when your attention wanders again.

pages.title: Nia makes one useful distinction
paragraphs: Nia asks whether the joke contained a hurtful remark that needs an apology. She remembers no such content and has no new information about the quiet response. She writes one brief note to listen more carefully at the next group, then returns to dinner.

The memory returns twice. Nia notices it and returns to the conversation at the table. The exercise is not disproved by the thought returning. The relevant observation is whether Nia can re-engage with the activity she chose.
key_messages: Nia checks for a specific hurt that needs repair and identifies no new evidence of one.
She decides to listen more carefully at the next group and then returns to the conversation at dinner.
When the memory returns, she redirects attention again rather than restarting the whole analysis.

pages.title: When there is an actionable concern
paragraphs: Jules realises they made a specific hurtful remark. Which response fits?

options.text: Label every concern as rumination and ignore it.
options.feedback: That could bypass a real responsibility. Distinguish an actionable issue from repetition about the whole self.

options.text: Decide on a proportionate apology, then notice and redirect repeated self-condemnation.
options.feedback: A practical repair and flexible attention can both be useful. Neither requires a guarantee about the other person’s response.

options.text: Keep replaying until no shame remains before acting.
options.feedback: Waiting for a feeling to disappear can delay a reasonable action and keep the loop going.

pages.title: Explain it without looking
paragraphs: Take a moment to answer in your own words before revealing the suggested reasoning.

questions.prompt: How can you distinguish reflection from rumination?
questions.answer: Ask whether the thinking produces new information, a concrete decision, or useful learning. Repeated abstract self-judgment often does not.

questions.prompt: What if a thought returns after redirecting attention?
questions.answer: Notice it and return again. The goal is flexible engagement, not proving that a thought can never appear.

pages.title: Lab: notice, decide, return
paragraphs: Use Nia’s joke example or a mild everyday replay. You may stop or use the fictional story if personal reflection becomes uncomfortable.
fields: What is the repeated question?
Is there new information or a practical action?
If needed, what one proportionate step fits?
What present activity will receive attention?
In the story, Nia’s memory returns twice. What does she do, and how could she tell whether it helped her rejoin the conversation?
pages.example:
Repeated question — “Why did I say that?”
Check — The quiet response supplies no new facts about whether anyone was hurt.
Action — Nia decides to listen more carefully next time.
Chosen activity — Nia returns to the conversation at dinner.
Result — The thought returns twice. Each time Nia notices it and rejoins the conversation.
pages.review: Check that redirecting attention does not bypass an important practical problem. Avoid judging success by whether the mind stayed blank.
pages.comparison: Compare your action and result fields. What did Nia do about the possible concern, and what showed she was able to rejoin dinner?

sources.title: CCI: worry and rumination — attention training and uncertainty

chapters.evidence_note: Attention practices can be useful, but persistent or intrusive thinking may require tailored support. This lesson does not establish the cause of any individual’s repetitive thoughts.

chapters.title: The rules underneath
chapters.story: The rule ‘I must never disappoint anyone’ leads to overcommitment and resentment.
chapters.learn: Explore conditional assumptions, core beliefs, and the costs of rigid personal rules.
chapters.lab: Identify a recurring rule and develop a more flexible version to test.

pages.title: The rules underneath
paragraphs: Jules agrees to bring extra materials, design another poster, and cover a session despite a full week. “If I disappoint someone, I am selfish,” they think. Resentment builds, and they eventually cancel at the last minute.
The same rule appears in several situations. It may once have helped Jules stay connected or avoid conflict. Now its rigid form seems to make honest planning harder.
key_messages: Jules accepts several tasks despite a full week, then cancels at the last minute.
The rule “If I disappoint someone, I am selfish” may help explain why Jules takes on too many tasks.
Ask what the rule might protect, such as connection, and what it costs, such as making realistic commitments harder.

pages.title: Identify the rule
paragraphs: Which statement is a conditional personal rule rather than a specific event or emotion?

options.text: Jules agreed to bring extra paper.
options.feedback: This describes an action. A rule would express a broader demand or an if-then assumption.

options.text: Jules feels resentful.
options.feedback: This names a feeling. It may signal an unmet need, but it is not itself the underlying rule.

options.text: If I disappoint anyone, it means I am selfish.
options.feedback: This links an event to a broad conclusion about identity. It is a candidate rule to investigate, not a fact to accept.

pages.title: Thoughts can reflect broader assumptions
paragraphs: An automatic thought belongs to a moment: “I cannot say no to this request.” A conditional assumption expresses a rule: “If I refuse, I will lose people.” A core belief is a broader view of self, others, or the world, such as “I am not worth caring about.”

These are different levels of a possible formulation. Do not assume a core belief simply because a behaviour repeats. Ask the person what the situation means, look for patterns, and remain open to context and alternative explanations.

diagram.title: Three levels of a possible pattern

items.label: Rule
items.detail: If I refuse, I will lose people

key_messages: An automatic thought belongs to one moment. A conditional assumption is a wider rule, such as “If I refuse, I will lose people.”
A core belief is a broader view of self, others, or the world.
A formulation is a working explanation of how a pattern fits together. Check it with the person and leave room for other explanations.

pages.title: Make a rule more flexible and test it
paragraphs: A flexible rule keeps a value without turning it into an impossible demand. Jules values reliability. “I can be considerate and honest about capacity” allows planning, negotiation, and occasional disappointment.

A new sentence does not automatically change a long-standing belief. Look for small experiences that fit or challenge it, and practise acting consistently with it. Some beliefs are connected to difficult histories that deserve more support than a short self-study exercise.

diagram.title: Keep the value; soften the demand

key_messages: Keep the value of reliability while softening an impossible demand.
Jules tries a flexible guide. “I can be considerate and honest about what I have time to do.”
Try a small action that fits the guide and observe the result. A long-standing belief may take more time and support.

pages.title: Jules tries a different response
paragraphs: Jules replies, “I can bring the paper, but I cannot cover the session this week.” The organiser finds another volunteer. Jules feels guilty at first, but keeps their feasible commitment.

This experience supports a more flexible possibility: setting one limit can coexist with being helpful. It does not guarantee every person will welcome a boundary. Jules can examine an unfavourable response without deciding their needs are illegitimate.
key_messages: Jules agrees to bring paper but declines to cover an extra session.
The organiser finds someone else, and Jules keeps the feasible commitment.
A boundary can coexist with helpfulness, though not every response will be favourable.

pages.title: Avoid over-interpreting behaviour
paragraphs: Alex hesitates before accepting an invitation. Can you conclude Alex has the core belief “I am unwanted”?

options.text: No. Ask what the hesitation means; tiredness, logistics, preference, or several beliefs could fit.
options.feedback: The outward behaviour does not uniquely identify a hidden belief. A formulation needs the person’s own account and context.

options.text: Yes. Hesitation is enough to reveal the belief.
options.feedback: That assigns a private meaning without evidence and can miss practical explanations.

options.text: No beliefs can ever influence behaviour.
options.feedback: Beliefs may influence behaviour, but recognising that possibility is different from knowing which belief is present.

pages.title: Explain it without looking
paragraphs: Take a moment to answer in your own words before revealing the suggested reasoning.

questions.prompt: How does a rule differ from a momentary thought?
questions.answer: A rule applies across situations, often as a should, must, or if-then statement. A thought occurs in a particular moment.

questions.prompt: What makes a more flexible rule useful?
questions.answer: It is believable, preserves an important value, allows context and limits, and suggests an action that can be tested.

pages.title: Lab: turn a demand into a guide
paragraphs: Use Jules’s commitments. You can work entirely with this fictional example.
fields: What repeated should, must, or if-then rule appears?
What value or need might it be trying to protect?
What are its benefits and costs in this situation?
What more flexible guide fits the evidence?
What small action could test it, and what would you review?
pages.example:
Rule — “If I disappoint someone, I am selfish.”
Value — Jules wants to be considerate and reliable.
Benefit and cost — Accepting tasks may avoid an awkward refusal. Taking on too much makes it harder to keep promises.
Flexible guide — “I can be considerate and honest about what I have time for.”
Test — Offer to bring paper and decline the extra session. Review what happened and whether Jules could keep the commitment.
pages.review: A flexible guide should not become another absolute demand to perform perfectly. Leave room for mixed reactions and learning.
pages.comparison: Compare your value, flexible guide and test. How could Jules protect reliability and learn whether the new commitment fits their week?

chapters.evidence_note: Core beliefs and assumptions are formulation concepts, not labels to impose on someone. Deeply distressing beliefs may be better explored with a qualified practitioner.

chapters.title: Working with a complicated situation
chapters.story: Someone faces both unfair treatment and harsh self-judgment.
chapters.learn: Combine CBT skills with boundaries, support, and changes to circumstances.
chapters.lab: Decide what calls for checking an interpretation, practical action, accepting uncertainty, or seeking help.

pages.title: Working with a complicated situation
paragraphs: At work, Nia is repeatedly assigned unpopular late shifts despite an agreed rotation. When she asks about it, her manager dismisses the concern. Nia thinks, “I am powerless, so there is no point speaking up.”

The rota provides evidence of a real imbalance. At the same time, “there is no possible action” is a broader conclusion. Nia needs an approach that respects the actual working conditions and the possible costs of challenging them.
key_messages: Nia’s work schedule, or rota, repeatedly assigns her unpopular late shifts outside the agreed rotation. Her manager dismisses her concern.
The rota shows an imbalance. Nia’s options may be limited and she does not yet know what support exists.
Consider her priorities, constraints, safety, and available support.

pages.title: Choose the starting point
paragraphs: Which response takes the documented rota problem and Nia’s circumstances into account?

options.text: Assume the manager must have a good reason.
options.feedback: That invents a reassuring explanation and can minimise the documented imbalance.

options.text: Acknowledge the evidence and explore Nia’s priorities, safety, support, and practical options.
options.feedback: This keeps the real circumstances central. It also allows specific thoughts to be examined without denying unfairness.

options.text: Tell Nia that feeling powerless proves she has no choices.
options.feedback: The feeling is understandable but does not by itself establish every possible option. Options may still be limited and costly.

pages.title: Match the tool to the situation
paragraphs: Different parts of a situation may call for different responses. Check an interpretation when evidence is ambiguous. Use problem-solving for a changeable task. Consider boundaries, support, or appropriate advice for a real interpersonal or structural problem.

CBT skills do not require accepting mistreatment or taking responsibility for another person’s actions. Emotional responses can be understandable signals. A useful formulation includes the environment, power, access to resources, and the costs of each option.
key_messages: Check interpretations when the evidence is ambiguous.
Use practical problem-solving for a changeable obstacle.
Real unfairness may call for boundaries, support, or appropriate advice.
Include power and circumstances when deciding which response fits.

pages.title: Agency can be partial
paragraphs: Nia may not control the manager’s response. She might control whether to keep a record, consult a trusted representative, request a meeting, or seek other advice. None of those options is automatically safe or available in every workplace.

A specific alternative to “I am powerless” could be “My options are constrained; I can find out what support exists before deciding.” This preserves the constraints and identifies a possible next step. It is not a promise that speaking up will fix the situation.

items.label: Known facts
items.detail: The rota departs from the agreement

items.label: Unknown outcomes
items.detail: How a challenge will be received

key_messages: Separate known facts, unknown outcomes, and possible influence.
Nia cannot control her manager’s response; her options may be constrained.
Nia might check what support exists before deciding whether to act. What is available depends on her workplace.

pages.title: A plan with context
paragraphs: Nia checks the rota and the written agreement, then privately asks a trusted staff representative about options. She considers potential consequences before deciding whether to make a formal request.
Nia also notices the thought “If this is happening, I must deserve it.” The rota does not support that conclusion. Challenging self-blame and addressing the working conditions can proceed together.
key_messages: Nia checks the rota and agreement, then privately explores support options.
The rota shows how shifts were allocated. It gives Nia no reason to blame herself.
Address the circumstances and examine self-blame together.

pages.title: A mixed situation
paragraphs: Jules receives fair criticism about a missed deadline and also a personal insult. Which response best fits?

options.text: Reject all feedback because the insult makes every criticism false.
options.feedback: The insult is inappropriate, but the deadline issue may still need a practical response. Separate the claims.

options.text: Accept the insult as proof that the criticism is accurate.
options.feedback: A personal attack is not established by a specific missed commitment. Keep behaviour, evidence, and identity separate.

options.text: Address the missed deadline and consider a boundary or support about the insult.
options.feedback: This distinguishes a practical responsibility from unacceptable treatment. Several tools may fit different parts of the same event.

pages.title: Explain it without looking
paragraphs: Take a moment to answer in your own words before revealing the suggested reasoning.

questions.prompt: Why include the environment in a CBT formulation?
questions.answer: Real demands, resources, discrimination, power, and support affect experiences and options. A thought-only account can miss important causes and constraints.

questions.prompt: Can checking self-blame and seeking practical support happen together?
questions.answer: Yes. Examining an unsupported personal conclusion does not require denying a real problem or delaying appropriate support.

pages.title: Lab: choose the tool, explain the fit
paragraphs: Use Nia’s rota example. Consider several responses rather than assuming one tool must solve everything.
fields: What facts indicate a real problem?
What interpretation goes beyond those facts?
Which parts are within Nia’s influence?
What practical support or advice might be appropriate?
What first step fits Nia’s priorities and possible risks?
pages.example:
Facts — The rota departs from an agreed shift rotation and the manager dismisses Nia’s concern.
Interpretation — “There is no possible action” is broader than those facts.
Influence — Nia can consider gathering records or checking support. The manager’s response remains unknown.
Support — A trusted staff representative may be able to explain options.
First step — If it fits her circumstances, privately ask about those options before deciding whether to raise the issue formally.
pages.review: Does the plan respect actual constraints? Do not treat a person’s inability to change a structural problem as a failure to use CBT.
pages.comparison: Compare the facts, possible influence and first step. Which details make it a real workplace problem, and what information would help Nia decide what to do?

chapters.evidence_note: The fictional workplace example teaches tool selection, not employment advice. Practical and professional support may be essential; no outcome is guaranteed.

chapters.title: Becoming your own investigator
chapters.story: An old pattern returns during a stressful week.
chapters.learn: Review learning, recognise early warning signs, and plan for setbacks.
chapters.lab: Create a learning summary and a realistic plan for responding when difficulties return.

pages.title: Becoming your own investigator
paragraphs: Several weeks later, Alex has used clearer checking standards and small social steps. Then a busy week disrupts sleep and routines. Alex notices the signup list being checked repeatedly again.

“I am back at the beginning,” they think. But Alex now notices the pattern earlier, can explain part of the loop, and knows a response that has helped before. A returning difficulty and losing all learning are not the same event.
key_messages: A busy week disrupts Alex’s routines, and repeated checking returns.
Alex thinks “I am back at the beginning.” This time they notice the pattern earlier and remember a way to respond.
A pattern can return even when someone has learned to recognise it sooner.

pages.title: Read the setback carefully
paragraphs: Which conclusion best fits the information?

options.text: The pattern has returned under strain; Alex can use what they have learned and reassess what support is needed.
