options.feedback: This acknowledges the difficulty without erasing previous learning. The next step can be specific and manageable.

options.text: Any returning worry proves the course has failed.
options.feedback: A single recurrence does not establish that no learning occurred. This course is not a treatment with a promised symptom outcome.

options.text: Ignore the checking because progress means nothing can go wrong now.
options.feedback: That dismisses new information. A useful maintenance plan includes noticing and responding to changes.

pages.title: Make a personal learning summary
paragraphs: A maintenance plan records what you have learned about a pattern, early signs that it is intensifying, small responses that fit, and sources of support. It should be short enough to use when things are difficult.

Alex’s early signs include repeated checks without new information, missed breaks, and the thought “I must be completely certain.” Their first response might be to revisit the agreed checking standard, simplify an overloaded day, and speak to someone supportive.
key_messages: A maintenance plan names the pattern and its early signs.
Choose one feasible response, a review point, and sources of support.
Keep the plan short enough to use during a difficult week.

pages.title: Review patterns without turning life into a test
paragraphs: Progress can include noticing earlier, choosing a more workable action, asking for support, or recovering from a difficult day more flexibly. A course score or streak cannot capture all of that.

Plan a brief revisit after using a skill and another at a useful later point. Adjust the timing to your circumstances. If difficulties persist, worsen, or substantially affect daily life, consider support from a qualified professional. You do not have to complete more exercises before asking.
key_messages: Progress can mean noticing earlier, choosing a workable action, or asking for support.
Review at a useful time and adapt to current capacity.
Persistent, worsening, or substantially disruptive difficulties deserve professional support.

pages.title: Alex’s one-page plan
paragraphs: Pattern: doubt followed by extra checking and short relief. Early signs: three returns to an unchanged list and a skipped break. First steps: check the actual task standard, pause the extra work, and review the week’s capacity.

Support: ask the organiser to clarify priorities; contact a qualified practitioner if the pattern becomes persistent or substantially disruptive. Review: after the next ordinary task, record what happened and update the plan. The plan guides a response; it does not promise that doubt will disappear.
key_messages: Alex’s early signs are repeated checks of an unchanged list and missed breaks.
Alex plans to check which work the task requires and what is feasible this week.
Alex can ask the organiser to clarify priorities. After the next task, they’ll review what happened and adjust the plan.

pages.title: Bring the skills together
paragraphs: After a stressful week, Nia has less energy and starts replaying a conversation. What is the best next step?

options.text: Complete every worksheet immediately to catch up.
options.feedback: An overloaded response may ignore current capacity. Choose the tool that fits the immediate pattern.

options.text: Map the current situation, choose one feasible response, and consider whether more support is needed.
options.feedback: This combines observation, tool selection, and context. It does not require starting the entire course again.

options.text: Use thought challenging for every feeling regardless of the cause.
options.feedback: Different problems call for different responses. Rest, practical help, or attention shifting may fit better.

pages.title: Explain it without looking
paragraphs: Take a moment to answer in your own words before revealing the suggested reasoning.

questions.prompt: What should a maintenance plan contain?
questions.answer: A short description of the pattern, early signs, feasible responses, a review point, and sources of support.

questions.prompt: What can show learning even when a difficulty returns?
questions.answer: Earlier recognition, more specific understanding, a more flexible action, or seeking useful support. Absence of all difficult feelings is not the standard.

pages.title: Lab: a plan for the next difficult week
paragraphs: Use Alex’s pattern, or create an optional personal summary. Keep it brief and realistic. Then try the final case to practise choosing tools without a chapter label.
fields: What pattern and trigger do you want to recognise?
What two early signs are observable?
What small first response has a clear purpose?
Who or what could provide support?
When will you review, and what would tell you more help is needed?
pages.example:
Pattern and trigger — A busy week disrupts routines and Alex starts checking the signup list repeatedly.
Early signs — Reopening the unchanged list and missing planned breaks.
First response — Revisit the agreed checking standard so Alex knows when the task is complete.
Support — Ask the organiser to clarify priorities. Seek qualified support if the pattern persists or disrupts daily life.
Review — After the next ordinary task, note whether the new plan met the agreed standard and left time for a break.
pages.review: Use this as a flexible guide. A return of difficulty is information, not a moral failure or a requirement to cope alone.
pages.comparison: Compare your early signs, first response and review point. Would each be specific enough for Alex to recognise or use during a busy week?

sources.title: CCI: worry and rumination — self management plan

chapters.evidence_note: Maintenance planning supports continuing learning. This course has not been tested for prevention of relapse or for clinical outcomes; recurrent symptoms deserve appropriate assessment and support.

cases.title: Checkpoint 1 · The unread invitation
story: Rowan receives an invitation to a community book group. They think, “I will have nothing useful to say,” notice tension without describing where they feel it, and leave it unanswered. Not replying brings relief that evening. A week later Rowan feels more isolated and believes they would not fit in.
tasks: Map the moment
In Your response, list the event, thought and action. What does “tense” tell you about Rowan’s experience? Which details would you still ask about?

The invitation is the event. “I will have nothing useful to say” is Rowan’s thought. Leaving the invitation unanswered is the action. Rowan reports tension. Ask what emotion they felt and what physical sensations they noticed before filling in either detail.
Explain a possible cycle
Compare how Rowan feels that evening and a week later. How might leaving the invitation unanswered connect those two experiences?
Avoiding the reply brings relief but prevents new information and a possible connection. Later isolation may strengthen the initial prediction. This is a hypothesis, not proof of the only cause.
Write a balanced account
What can Rowan fairly conclude from the available facts?
The invitation does not establish how a visit would go. Rowan can acknowledge uncertainty and consider a small information-gathering step if participation fits their interests.
rubric: The cycle includes immediate and later consequences.
Missing information stays open rather than being invented.

cases.title: Checkpoint 2 · Asking at the library
story: Rowan wants to ask a librarian whether a beginner book group is suitable. They predict, “The librarian will laugh or say my question is stupid.” Rowan usually asks a friend to speak for them. The library is an ordinary setting they have safely visited before.
tasks: Design the experiment
Write the question Rowan could choose to ask. What words or actions would count as ridicule? What support needs to stay in place?

Rowan could choose to ask one clear suitability question. Observe words and actions, not hidden opinions. Preserve any communication accommodations; consider voluntarily changing only the friend speaking on their behalf if that fits Rowan’s needs.
Interpret a brief response
The librarian says, “Yes, beginners are welcome,” then turns to another visitor. Did the predicted ridicule occur? What can Rowan conclude about the visit, and what is still unknown?
The predicted explicit ridicule did not occur in this trial. A brief answer does not establish a private opinion. Rowan obtained information while possibly still anxious.
Interpret an awkward response
Now imagine the librarian says, “It is on the sign.” Compare those words with Rowan’s prediction of laughter or an insult. What would you conclude from this version, and what could Rowan do next?

This may be unhelpful or brusque, but it is not identical to explicit ridicule. Note the exact response, consider its limits, and decide whether another source of information or a different next step is useful.
rubric: Support and access needs are respected.
Both favourable and awkward results permit specific learning.

cases.title: Final case · The first book-group session
story: Rowan attends the group and answers one question briefly. Another participant interrupts twice. Afterwards the organiser thanks Rowan for coming. At home Rowan thinks, “Nobody wants me there,” replays the interruptions, and decides never to return.
Rowan also has a genuine scheduling problem: the next meeting overlaps a regular care commitment. They feel tired and have stopped a short reading routine they used to enjoy.
New information arrives: the organiser says interruptions have affected other participants too and proposes a turn-taking format. The organiser cannot change the next meeting’s time.
tasks: Map without mind-reading
Separate observations, interpretations, feelings, actions, and unknowns.

Observations include two interruptions and thanks from the organiser. “Nobody wants me” is broader than the evidence. Fatigue is reported; ask about other bodily and emotional experiences rather than inventing them.
Identify a possible loop
What might withdrawal and repeated analysis accomplish now and cost later?
Withdrawal may offer relief while limiting connection and new information. Replaying without new facts may take time from rest. Neither explanation removes the real interruptions or care commitment.
Choose tools that fit
Select responses for the interpretation, interruptions, scheduling, and reduced activity.

Examine the global rejection thought; consider a boundary or organiser support about interruptions; problem-solve the scheduling constraint; consider a manageable reading activity if Rowan values it. Do not treat every issue as a thinking error.
Design one small experiment
Using the facts available so far, write a voluntary action Rowan could take, a prediction you could observe, and what two possible outcomes would tell you.

If Rowan wants to return and finds a meeting they can attend, they might make one short contribution. They predict they will be interrupted before they finish. Finishing would show a contribution was possible on that occasion. An interruption would show what happened that time and could help Rowan decide whether to ask the organiser for support.
Update with new information
Read the organiser’s message above. Which part of your original account would you revise? Name one obstacle that remains and one change Rowan could now consider.

Other participants were interrupted too, which gives Rowan another way to understand the interruptions. The turn-taking format could change how long members get to speak. The next meeting still conflicts with Rowan’s care commitment.
Plan for a difficult week
Write an early sign, one feasible response, and a source of support.

An early sign could be repeated replay replacing rest. A response could be one practical decision and a return to a chosen activity. Support might include a trusted person or professional help if difficulties persist or substantially interfere.
rubric: Reasoning stays specific to the evidence.
Several tools are matched to distinct problems.
The experiment is voluntary, safe, and observable.
The maintenance plan recognises capacity and support.

scope: This draft introduces cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) skills to adults with no psychology background. Diagnosis, individual treatment and professional training are outside its scope. A practitioner review and learner pilot are still pending.

characters.name: Alex
characters.description: A volunteer who wants to contribute without getting trapped in repeated checking.

characters.name: Nia
characters.description: A shift worker making room for creativity, rest, and fair treatment.

characters.name: Jules
characters.description: A drawing-group member practising clearer requests and realistic commitments.
